profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a health sciences librarian and a medical education editor who are preparing an internal workshop package based on the PRISMA 2020 explanation-and-elaboration article for researchers at a university hospital. The package will be used for a 90-minute training session next month and must include a slide deck, a handout, and a worked example. The agenda is to decide what materials will be produced, how the PRISMA 2020 article will be translated into teachable content, who will prepare each component, and what needs to be ready by the end of the week. The expected outcome is a division of responsibilities and a shared timeline for a 'complete draft' of the workshop materials.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Systematic review methods, database searching, reporting guidance, research training
members.background: Maya supports clinical and public health teams on evidence synthesis projects and frequently teaches search strategy documentation and PRISMA flow reporting to fellows and residents.
members.private_state: She wants the workshop materials to be methodologically careful enough that faculty can reuse them later, and she is concerned about being blamed if the examples oversimplify PRISMA guidance or if the handout omits operational details participants need.
hidden_assumptions: A 'worked example' for PRISMA teaching should walk through one review from search strategy to flow diagram to checklist entries, even if some later checklist items are only briefly illustrated.
When someone says the materials need a 'complete draft' by Friday, that means content-complete and ready for internal review, not visually polished.
The 'PRISMA article' everyone is using as the source means the BMJ explanation-and-elaboration paper with the 27-item checklist details and published exemplars.
A participant 'handout' for this kind of workshop normally includes practical fill-in aids such as a checklist table and example wording, not just summary notes.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: Curriculum packaging, faculty workshop production, instructional editing, slide-based teaching materials
members.background: Alex works in the hospital's education office turning technical content into faculty-ready sessions and usually manages deadlines, branding, and distribution formats for continuing education events.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, low-friction workshop package that can be finalized quickly and distributed without heavy revision, and he is worried that Maya may create overly dense materials that exceed what faculty will actually use in a 90-minute session.
hidden_assumptions: A 'worked example' in a workshop package usually means one or two annotated reporting excerpts embedded in slides rather than a full end-to-end review walkthrough.
When people ask for a 'complete draft' by Friday, they mean a near-final package with layout, formatting, and session-ready files that stakeholders can approve directly.

The 'PRISMA article' in this context is the core statement-and-guidance package already circulated by the education office, and the detailed explanation paper is simply background support rather than the main teaching source.
A workshop 'handout' generally means a concise two-page takeaway summarizing key points from the slides, since participants are not expected to fill it out during the session.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the worked example
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include a 'worked example' in the workshop package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means a single review traced across multiple PRISMA 2020 elements, including search documentation, study flow, and sample checklist phrasing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means a compact annotated example showing a few polished excerpts from a published review to illustrate reporting style.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In training contexts, 'worked example' sounds standard and mutually intelligible, and both versions plausibly support the workshop, so neither person feels a need to define the term.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of complete draft by Friday
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that a 'complete draft' should be ready by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the Friday milestone is met if all substantive content exists in rough form, with citations, examples, and notes for later formatting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the Friday milestone is met only if the deck, handout, and example are formatted, branded, and coherent enough to send directly to faculty leads.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use milestone language informally, and because both are competent planners accustomed to draft iterations, the phrase 'complete draft' feels sufficiently precise without discussing acceptance criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: Which PRISMA article is the shared source
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to building the materials around 'the PRISMA 2020 article.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is specifically thinking of the explanation-and-elaboration article with bullet-point recommendations and published exemplars for each item.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the condensed statement/checklist package already circulated internally, treating the longer explanation paper as optional background.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The article family has closely related titles and is routinely discussed under the umbrella label 'PRISMA 2020,' so each assumes the same document is in view.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the session needs a 'handout' for participants.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the handout includes the checklist items, a fillable reporting aid, and at least one example phrasing block participants can adapt for their own reviews.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the handout is a short summary companion to the slides, excluding worksheets or reusable authoring tools.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A handout is an ordinary workshop artifact whose exact boundary is usually left implicit, and both versions sound reasonable enough that the phrase does not trigger clarification.

turns.inner_thought: I want us anchored in the explanation-and-elaboration paper, because that's where the operational detail lives. For this to be reusable by faculty later, the package can't just be high-level. The worked example should carry one review across the session so people can see how the search, flow diagram, and reporting language connect. And the handout needs to be something participants can actually use afterward, not just a recap.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think the goal is to turn the PRISMA 2020 article into a practical 90-minute workshop package for our researchers, with a slide deck, a handout, and a worked example that all fit together.

turns.inner_thought: The big thing is getting to something faculty can react to immediately. If Friday's draft isn't basically session-ready, we'll lose time in revisions. I need a clean package, not a pile of content notes that still has to be shaped.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. From my side, the main thing is making sure a complete draft is ready by Friday so the faculty leads can react quickly and we can keep the session streamlined.

turns.inner_thought: I'll frame it around the 27 items and pull from the explanation bullets and exemplars in the BMJ explanation paper. That gives enough substance to avoid oversimplifying, even if we only emphasize selected items in the live session.
turns.utterance: One way to structure it would be around the 27 PRISMA items, using the explanation points and published exemplars from the PRISMA 2020 article so the teaching has a clear backbone.

turns.inner_thought: That works as long as I can shape it from the PRISMA 2020 article materials the office already circulated. I don't want to dump every nuance onto participants. The deck should stay selective and visually light.
turns.utterance: I like that. I can shape the deck from the PRISMA 2020 article materials we already have in circulation and make sure participants aren't getting overloaded with too much detail.

turns.inner_thought: If we use one published review all the way through, attendees will finally see how reporting decisions line up across sections instead of treating the checklist as disconnected boxes. That's what I mean by a worked example.
turns.utterance: For the worked example, I think it would help if we followed one published review across the session so attendees can see how the pieces connect.

turns.inner_thought: Great, a compact example thread. I'll reserve a few slides and use annotated excerpts so it stays elegant and fast. We definitely do not need to build the whole session around one review in exhaustive detail.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I'll reserve a few slides for the worked example and annotate it in a way that keeps things visually clean.

turns.inner_thought: I'll make the handout useful: checklist table, adaptable wording, and space people can use when translating their own reviews into PRISMA language. If we don't include that, they'll leave without enough practical support.
turns.utterance: I can draft the handout. I'd like it to give participants something practical they can use when they translate their own reviews into PRISMA language.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, I'll turn that into a concise takeaway that matches the deck. It should be short, branded, and easy to distribute after the session; I don't want it turning into a workbook.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll format the handout so it's a concise takeaway that matches the deck and is easy to distribute after the session.

turns.inner_thought: By Friday I can absolutely have all substantive content assembled: slide text, citations, worked example material, and the handout content in draft form. Formatting can come after; what matters is that the intellectual pieces are there for review.
turns.utterance: I can have the substantive content for the slides, handout, and worked example assembled by Friday, with citations and example text in place, so we have a complete draft.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Once her draft comes in, I can do a quick polish pass and then send it on. Hopefully it already looks coherent enough that I'm just tightening, not rebuilding.
turns.utterance: Friday should work well. Once the complete draft is in, I'll do a quick final pass so it's ready to send onward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll pull directly from the explanation-and-elaboration paper and map those details into the slides, the handout, and the worked example. That way the package is careful enough to stand up if faculty reuse it later.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll pull material directly from the PRISMA 2020 article and map it into the workshop components so the deck, handout, and worked example stay aligned.

turns.inner_thought: Sounds settled: she develops the content, I package and circulate. By Friday I expect a near-final workshop set I can brand, check, and send to faculty leads without major redesign.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll handle the packaging and review circulation, and we'll treat Friday as the point when the complete draft is ready for that next step.
